name: Zamboanga Chabacano
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand sources agree (1 agree, 1 refine), none contradicts
catalog_citation: Steinkrüger, Patrick O. 2013. Zamboanga Chabacano. In: Michaelis, S.M., Maurer, P., Haspelmath, M. & Huber, M. (eds.), Atlas of Pidgin and Creole Language Structures Online (APiCS Online), survey chapter 46. Leipzig: MPI-EVA. https://apics-online.info/surveys…
catalog_locator: APiCS Online survey chapter 46, section 4 'Phonology' (paragraph after Table 2 Consonants)
catalog_quote: Word stress is distinctive; for example: nadá ‘to swim’ (< Spanish nadar) vs. náda ‘nothing’ (< Spanish nada). Orthography is more or less anarchic and follows mixed principles: Sometimes it follows the system of Spanish, sometimes that of English, and sometimes that of Tagalog (Pilipino). Neither word stress nor accent is usually indicated (in contrast to the spelling system used in this article and the database).

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding APiCS quotation is verbatim in the survey text we hold at the stated place (sec. 4 Phonology, after Table 2). (2) Deciding source is a 2013 specialist grammar sketch (7 pp) with a one-line stress statement; the classification lexical is consistent with how the catalog codes Spanish (stan1288 = lexical) and Tagalog/Hiligaynon (lexical). (3) Two open sources downloaded now corroborate: Lipski & Santoro 2007 (contrastive nada/nadá; 'accentuation rules are those of standard Spanish', i.e. a Spanish-type default with lexical exceptions -- refines, does not contradict) and Lesho 2014 ('all previous descriptions indicate that Chabacano has lexical stress'; three-syllable window; noun-penult vs verb-final pairs, matching Riego de Dios 1989's rightward stress shift already held). (4) The best primary descriptions (Forman 1972, Ing 1968, Ing 1967) are not yet obtained and not open

sources.quote: 'Stress is a matter of syllable prominence (loudness and possibly length), and is significant at grammatical levels (nada 'nothing' vs nadá 'swim'). Generally speaking, accentuation rules are those of standard Spanish. ... Accents, however, have been omitted where predictable.'
sources.locator: preprint p.5 (introduction, paragraph before sec. 1 'Unmarked Verbs')
sources.note: Independent specialist statement: stress contrastive (nada/nadá) and 'accentuation rules are those of standard Spanish' -- adds the Spanish-type default our the primary-stress rule says is unstated.

sources.quote: p.51: 'All previous descriptions indicate that Chabacano has lexical stress.' p.53: 'Ing (1968) includes some descriptions of how lexical stress in Zamboanga Chabacano is realized in compound words, short phrases, and longer sentences. He describes stress as often neutralized in phrases above the word level, with only the last word ... receiving its typical pitch prominence.' pp.182-183 (Cavite): 'Cavite Chabacano has lexical stress (Ramos 1963:66-67)' with minimal pairs /ˈna.da/ 'nothing' vs /na.ˈda/ 'to swim', /ˈka.sa/ vs /ka.ˈsa/; stress on ult, penult or antepenult; 'Stress does not occur
sources.locator: p.51 (ch.2 literature review), p.53 (on Ing 1968 for Zamboanga), pp.182-183 sec. 5.6.2 'Word level prosody' (Cavite variety)
sources.note: Only instrumental work on any Chabacano variety (Cavite, same glottocode); literature review confirms 'all previous descriptions indicate lexical stress', gives the three-syllable window, and summarizes Ing 1968 on Zamboanga stress.
